Extending ggplot3d

Source: vignettes/articles/extending.Rmd
extending.Rmd

Every layer drawn in coord_3d() hands its geometry to the panel’s scene as a scene packet: typed tables of vertices, faces, polylines, markers and text. The scene merges the packets of all layers and resolves visibility across them, so a new geom only describes its geometry and never draws anything itself. This article writes a geom that draws one triangle per group of three rows. It assumes familiarity with ggproto extensions; Visibility explains what the scene does with the packets.

  1. Define the geom with ggplot2::ggproto().

  2. Emit its geometry as a packet with new_scene_packet().

  3. Register the emitter with register_geom_3d().

  4. Add the layer to a plot with layer_3d().

library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)

The scene packet

A packet holds columnar tables. vertices gives positions, corners lists the vertex of each face corner in order, faces says where each face starts in the corner table (offset) and how many corners it has (count), and styles holds the fill and outline colours that faces refer to by style_id. Indices start at 1. An empty packet shows every table with its columns.

new_scene_packet()

Positions in a packet are normalised to the panel box, which runs from 0 to 1 along each axis. normalise_homogeneous_3d() does that conversion from data units given the panel ranges. A fourth homogeneous coordinate w = 0 marks a point at infinity in a direction, which the engine clips to the box; the second point below is the direction of the positive x axis.

normalise_homogeneous_3d(c(5, 1), c(0, 0), c(1, 0), w = c(1, 0),
  ranges = list(x = c(0, 10), y = c(-1, 1), z = c(0, 2)))
#> $x
#> [1] 0.5 0.1
#> 
#> $y
#> [1] 0.5 0.0
#> 
#> $z
#> [1] 0.5 0.0
#> 
#> $w
#> [1] 1 0

An emitter

The geom itself declares its aesthetics like any ggplot2 geom. It needs no draw_panel() method, because coord_3d() never calls one for registered geoms.

GeomTriangle3D <- ggproto("GeomTriangle3D", Geom,
  required_aes = c("x", "y", "z"),
  default_aes = aes(fill = "#2E6F9E", alpha = 1),
  draw_key = draw_key_polygon)

The emitter receives the layer’s data after scales and statistics, with x, y and z already normalised to the panel box, plus two internal columns: .source, the input row of each record, and .layer, the layer index. It returns one packet. Writing source_row and layer_id into the packet lets the viewer and the alt text trace each face back to its data.

emit_triangle <- function(data, params, panel_params) {
  stopifnot(nrow(data) == 3L)
  new_scene_packet(
    vertices = list(x = as.double(data$x), y = as.double(data$y),
                    z = as.double(data$z)),
    corners = list(vertex = 1:3, source_row = as.integer(data$.source)),
    faces = list(offset = 1L, count = 3L, style_id = 1L,
                 source_row = as.integer(data$.source[1]),
                 layer_id = as.integer(data$.layer[1]), opacity = data$alpha[1]),
    styles = data.frame(style_id = 1L, fill = data$fill[1],
                        colour = NA_character_, shade = FALSE),
    panel_id = panel_params$panel_id)
}

Registering and using the geom

register_geom_3d() maps the geom class to its emitter. From then on any layer with that geom works in coord_3d(); layer_3d() adds a ggplot2 layer object to the plot.

register_geom_3d(GeomTriangle3D, emit_triangle, replace = TRUE)
triangle <- layer(geom = GeomTriangle3D, stat = "identity",
                  position = "identity", params = list())
corners <- data.frame(x = c(0, 1, 0), y = c(0, 0, 1), z = c(0, 1, 1))
ggplot(corners, aes(x, y, z = z)) + layer_3d(triangle) + coord_3d()

The triangle depth-sorts with the panel’s grid lines and back walls like any built-in layer, and a second layer that crosses it would be split where the two intersect.
